title: Review of c46's hunting-predators-divide-256 finding on fresh seed 10: predators crash the prey (49 -> 3), the prey re-form (49) and decline again (19), and predators divide after meals (12 persistent splits, 17 strict, 11 away from prey); prey do not divide (0)
summary: labkit run of the finding's world.py (defaults) on seed 10 at 256^2, T=12000, --lineage-k 5, and the finding's splits3.py at area >= 8 on both kinds. Prey bodies by t: 10 (t=0), 49 (t=2000), 3 (t=3000), 19, 49 (t=5000), 48, 44, 32, 36, 31, 23, 19 (t=12000); predators 47-59 after t=3000, 39 at the end. Predators: 30 splits, 12 persistent (generation 1), merge/split 0.1; strict test 17 splits, 11 with no prey within 6 px (strict_pred8.png: rods and Y-shapes pinching at t=7800-11800). Prey: 0 persistent splits, 0 strict.

observations.D: predator divisions after meals: 12 persistent splits (rerun256 FACTS), 17 strict, 11 away from prey (strict_pred8.png t=7800-11800); prey 0 (strict_prey8.json)

seeds_run.result: pass (predator D; one prey crash and recovery)

verdicts.limitation: Fewer predator splits and a shallower lineage than the author's seed 2 (12 vs 19 persistent, generation 1 vs 2); some strict 'splits' are dimming fragments of predators between meals (strip rows 3 and 7), so the strict count overstates clean fissions. The population dynamics show one crash and recovery, then a slow decline, not repeated cycles. Prey reappear by nucleation, not division. No matched predator-free twin in this review (one is in my review of the claim, 20261027T0153-c49-review-hunting-ecology).
